html:
The Battle of Verdun was fought from 21 February to 18 December 1916 around the fortress town of Verdun in northeast France. The French army held off a German attack in the longest battle of World War I.

The German commander Erich von Falkenhayn chose a place France would not give up. He later wrote that he meant to bleed the French army white; historians doubt that this was his plan from the start. The attack opened with the heaviest shelling yet seen, and Fort Douaumont fell in four days. General Philippe Pétain then organised the defence. He kept one road open for trucks, later called the Sacred Way, and moved divisions in and out, so that most of the French army served at Verdun. In summer Germany had to send troops to the Somme and against the Brusilov Offensive. In autumn the French took back the lost forts.

The front ended almost where it began. Together the two sides had about 700,000 killed, wounded and missing, some 300,000 of them dead. Verdun became the symbol of French endurance and of the waste of the war. Pétain became a hero, which helped him take power in 1940; see Vichy.
